summary:
Afghanistan under Taliban rule offers no legal protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the EUAA country-of-origin report of February 2026 finds this was true both before and after the 2021 takeover. Amnesty International's position, recorded in that report, is that same-sex relations are punishable by death.

Criminalisation operates in layers. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, updated 19 January 2026, states that Afghanistan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women: Penal Code 2017 provisions on sodomy and inciting sodomy carry up to two years' imprisonment, while the Code's Sharia-reference clause permits the death penalty for same-sex activity.

The Taliban's Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice Law of 31 July 2024 adds a preventive surveillance duty. Article 22 obliges the overseer to prevent listed evils including lesbianism and homosexuality 'even if with one's own spouse', codifying moral surveillance over same-sex conduct alongside adultery and gambling.

Enforcement is documented and escalating. OutRight International's February 2023 report, based on 22 interviews conducted between September and October 2022 with LGBTIQ Afghans still in the country, found Taliban security officials pursuing gay men and trans women more systematically than in the movement's earlier rule, with physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations; the Taliban Supreme Court has confirmed such punishments on social media. CNN reported in November 2024 that LGBTQ Afghans face beatings and sexual abuse in Taliban custody.

Human Rights Watch and OutRight's January 2022 report, based on 60 interviews with LGBT Afghans, found Taliban members and their supporters attacking, threatening and expelling LGBT people from their homes, with abuse by family, neighbours and partners surging after the takeover; many went into hiding or fled.

A DW feature of October 2021 profiled a trans man and a gay friend in their mid-20s hiding in Kabul after the takeover, stating that under Taliban rule LGBTQ people face the death penalty and their only option is to leave, and documenting street attacks on men read as gay.

JURIST's November 2024 feature, drawing on the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan, reports systematic persecution after August 2021, notes that even the post-2001 constitution provided no protective framework, and states that visibly transgender individuals face the gravest risks, including exploitation and violence.

The UN human-rights office reported in March 2026 that at least 1,110 people were flogged in 2025, nearly double the 2024 figure, and warned that women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for moral crimes such as adultery, illicit relationships and sodomy. That figure is a general count of corporal punishment, not a trans-specific rate, and no per-capita denominator is provided.
tangentialFactors:
The EUAA Country Guidance on Afghanistan treats LGBTIQ Afghans as persons perceived to transgress religious and social norms, alongside minors without support networks and persons facing the death penalty; this is the framework used to assess their protection claims in EU member states.

On 23 January 2025 the International Criminal Court's prosecutor, Karim Ahmad Khan, requested arrest warrants against Taliban leaders Hibatullah Akhundzada and Abdul Hakim Haqqani for persecution of women, girls and the LGBTQ community, the first time the court has recognised crimes against the LGBTQ community.
localsOnly:
Marriage and partnership recognition. Under the Islamic Republic, the 1971 Law of Marriages required a legal marriage to be between two Muslim adults of the opposite sex, with Article 41 directing that gaps in the law be resolved by Islamic law principles, so no same-sex marriage, civil union or domestic partnership was recognised. The 1949 Law on Marriages, Weddings and Circumcision likewise framed marriage as between a Muslim man and a woman. Under Taliban rule since 2021, same-sex relationships and marriages are not recognised at all.

Criminal code provisions. Article 430 made it 'Instigation of Delinquency' for an adult to promote or assist a minor in adultery, homosexuality or prostitution, a provision that can reach any adult, including a caregiver or partner; Article 427 increased punishment where the victim was under 18. Article 398 offered lesser punishment for vigilante honour killings that can target minors found engaging in homosexuality, and Article 373 imposes fines or murder-equivalent penalties for spreading a 'dangerous disease'. Under the Islamic Republic, persons convicted of homosexuality were generally sentenced to prison in the cities.

Discrimination and organisation. No law addressed discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and political parties were prohibited from advocating anything opposing Islamic morality. The 2017 U.S. State Department report found that LGBTI community members did not have access to certain health services and could be fired from jobs because of sexual orientation, and that organisations protecting LGBTI freedom remained underground because they could not legally register with the government; the 2020 report confirmed this.

Care access. Before 2003 little or no HIV-AIDS education or treatment existed; the 2008 official count was 504 people living with HIV-AIDS, though the true figure was suspected to be in the thousands. The first HIV-AIDS treatment centre opened in Kabul in 2009, access to anti-retroviral drugs is at best limited, and the 2020 report states that the government permits condom distribution only to married couples, excluding same-sex couples. Low literacy, weak infrastructure and social taboos impede public health education.

Bacha bazi. Teenage boys were kidnapped, dressed in women's clothing, made to dance in competitions and forced into sexual acts; militia members without access to women kidnapped boys to be humiliated and raped, and other boys became prostitutes regardless of sexual orientation. The practice was prevalent in big cities and reported in 2007 as still common in northern Afghanistan. US-backed Northern Alliance warlords kidnapped, trafficked and raped young boys after 2001, yet neither the U.S. Department of Defense nor the Afghan government acted despite awareness. President Hamid Karzai signed an agreement to ban the practice and a law prohibited Afghan soldiers from having their 'ashna' ('friend') live with them, but it was rarely enforced and police were reportedly complicit. The Taliban banned bacha bazi alongside homosexuality in 1996, both carrying the death penalty; under the Islamic Republic young victims were often charged rather than the adult perpetrators. Article 430 can deter adults from seeking care for minors.

Education and censorship. Low literacy, weak infrastructure, taboos and abstinence-only sex education programmes hamper access; Article 32 of the 2002 Press Law prohibits 'incitement to depravity' and Article 27(D) of the 1973 Postal Law bars material 'repugnant to public decency'. Hamid Zaher's 2009 memoir It Is Your Enemy Who Is Dock-Tailed cannot be distributed within the country. A 2011 survey found young men displaying rainbow symbols unaware of their meaning and quickly removing them; the 2017 and 2020 State Department reports noted that awareness of sexual orientation or gender identity remained limited and that homosexuality was widely seen as taboo.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2008 HIV-AIDS figure of 504 is an official count that the source itself treats as a suspected undercount; no reliable prevalence figure is available.

The 1,110 flogging figure for 2025 is a general count of corporal punishment, not a trans-specific rate, and no per-capita denominator is provided, so it cannot be used to compare severity across jurisdictions.

The inventory does not document entry or visa rules, passport or gender-marker policy, airport or border screening practice, or bathroom and facilities law for Afghanistan; those questions are unresolved here.

Enforcement data on prosecutions under the 2017 Penal Code and the 2024 morality law is not disaggregated; the sources report documented cases and testimony rather than systematic counts.
